raw_case_text:
A 13-year-old boy was referred to our hospital with complaints of high-grade fever, non-bilious, non-bloody projectile vomiting, light headedness, generalized weakness, reduced appetite and passing black-coloured urine. Prior to his admission, the child was febrile (40  C) with blood pressure of 110/40 mmHg (considered to be low as per guidelines of the National Institute of Health), along with thrombocytopaenia (28 000 mm-3 blood; normal: 1.5-4.5 mm-3 blood), low haematological parameters of haemoglobin (12.3 g dl-1; normal: 10-15.5 g dl-1), haematocrit (35.8 %; normal: 35-44 %), mean corpuscular volume (66.1 fl; normal: 80-95 fl) and mean corpuscular haemoglobin (22.7 pg; normal: 32-36 pg). Blood urea (62 mg dl-1; normal: 5-18 mg dl-1) and random blood sugar (204 mg dl-1; normal: 70-140 mg dl-1) levels were significantly raised. Peripheral blood smear examination was positive for P. vivax. Other tests such as Dengue (Non-structural protein 1) NS1, scrub typhus card tests, Widal test and COVID 19 reverse transcriptase (RT)-PCR were negative. Despite thrombocytopaenia, the child had no bleeding manifestations and was administered a first dose of intravenous artesunate and intravenous fluids.
With the impending hypovolaemia, and persistent hypotension with an episode of loss of consciousness for 20 min, the child was referred to our hospital. He was afebrile, hypotensive (88/36 mmHg), with high pulse rate (110 bpm) and facial swelling. There was reduction in urine output of around 150 ml per day, but the oxygen saturation (SpO2) was well maintained. Liver was enlarged up to 2 cm below the right costal margin. Other systemic examinations were within normal limits. Upon laboratory investigations, his haemoglobin level was 11 g dl-1, with a low haematocrit (34.2 %), mean corpuscular volume (71 fl) and mean corpuscular haemoglobin (22.9 pg) values with platelet count of 36 000 mm-3 blood. Serum direct bilirubin and liver enzymes were elevated. Giemsa-stained peripheral blood smears revealed normal sized erythrocytes with microgametocytes containing malarial pigments (Fig. 1). Quantitative buffy coat (QBC) examination detected gametocytes of non-falciparum species. Blood sample was subjected to a multiplex nested PCR assay using published primers (Table 1), and an amplified product of 121 bp corresponding with P. vivax was detected by 1.5 % agarose gel electrophoresis using a molecular ladder of 100 bp (Thermo Scientific Gene Ruler 100 bp ladder) (Fig. 2). Buffer used for the agarose gel cast and running buffer in the gel electrophoresis tank was 10x Tris boric acid EDTA (TBE). The child was treated with injectable inotropes, intravenous fluids, oxygenation, the remaining two doses of artesunate and injectable antibiotics (ceftriaxone and vancomycin). Antibiotics were discontinued after malaria was reported. A repeat complete haemogram showed a fall of platelets to 19 000 mm-3 blood after 7 h of treatment, but the child became stable after 22 h with the same regimen and was discharged with advice to continue artemether-lumefantrine combination without any other drugs and/or antibiotics.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 13-year-old boy was referred with high-grade fever, non-bilious non-bloody projectile vomiting, lightheadedness, generalized weakness, reduced appetite, passing black-colored urine, persistent hypotension, and a 20-minute episode of loss of consciousness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially presented to an outside facility with high-grade fever (40 °C), non-bilious, non-bloody projectile vomiting, lightheadedness, generalized weakness, reduced appetite, and black-colored urine. At the referring facility, he was found to have low blood pressure (110/40 mmHg), severe thrombocytopenia (28,000 mm^-3), microcytic hypochromic indices, elevated blood urea (62 mg dL^-1), and hyperglycemia (204 mg dL^-1), with a peripheral blood smear positive for Plasmodium vivax. He had no bleeding manifestations despite thrombocytopenia and received an initial dose of intravenous artesunate and intravenous fluids. Due to impending hypovolemia, persistent hypotension, and a 20-minute episode of loss of consciousness, he was referred to our hospital, where reduced urine output of approximately 150 mL per day was also noted.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, projectile vomiting, lightheadedness, generalized weakness, anorexia, dark/black urine, oliguria (~150 mL/day), and transient syncope/loss of consciousness. Pertinent negative: no bleeding manifestations.

objective.physical_examination: Prior to transfer, temperature was 40 °C and blood pressure was 110/40 mmHg. On admission to our hospital, the patient was afebrile, hypotensive (blood pressure 88/36 mmHg), and tachycardic (pulse rate 110 bpm), with well-maintained oxygen saturation (SpO2) and reduced urine output (~150 mL/day). General examination revealed facial swelling. Abdominal examination showed hepatomegaly with the liver palpable up to 2 cm below the right costal margin. Other systemic examinations were within normal limits.
objective.routine_investigations: Pre-referral investigations: platelet count 28,000 mm^-3 (normal: 1.5-4.5 lakh mm^-3), hemoglobin 12.3 g dL^-1 (normal: 10-15.5 g dL^-1), hematocrit 35.8% (normal: 35-44%), MCV 66.1 fL (normal: 80-95 fL), MCH 22.7 pg (normal: 32-36 pg), blood urea 62 mg dL^-1 (normal: 5-18 mg dL^-1), and random blood sugar 204 mg dL^-1 (normal: 70-140 mg dL^-1); peripheral blood smear positive for P. vivax; dengue NS1, scrub typhus card test, Widal test, and COVID-19 RT-PCR were all negative. Admission laboratory investigations at our hospital: hemoglobin 11 g dL^-1, hematocrit 34.2%, MCV 71 fL, MCH 22.9 pg, and platelet count 36,000 mm^-3 (falling to 19,000 mm^-3 after 7 hours of treatment). Serum direct bilirubin and liver enzymes were elevated. Giemsa-stained peripheral blood smears showed normal-sized erythrocytes with microgametocytes containing malarial pigments, and quantitative buffy coat (QBC) examination detected gametocytes of non-falciparum species.
objective.advanced_workup: Multiplex nested PCR assay of blood with 1.5% agarose gel electrophoresis (10x TBE buffer, 100 bp molecular ladder) detected an amplified 121 bp product corresponding to Plasmodium vivax.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe Plasmodium vivax malaria complicated by hypotensive shock and severe thrombocytopenia, confirmed by Giemsa-stained peripheral blood smear, QBC examination, and multiplex nested PCR (121 bp band for P. vivax). Dengue (NS1), scrub typhus, typhoid fever (Widal test), and COVID-19 (RT-PCR) were ruled out. Management included injectable inotropes, intravenous fluids, oxygen support, completion of the remaining two doses of intravenous artesunate, and empiric injectable ceftriaxone and vancomycin (which were discontinued once malaria was confirmed). Although platelets transiently dropped to 19,000 mm^-3 at 7 hours, the patient stabilized after 22 hours of treatment and was discharged on an oral artemether-lumefantrine combination without any additional antibiotics.
